correctness.summary: Bit packing produces corrupted output because the 32-bit `buffer` cannot hold the carry, and the post-flush shift `(int)((uint)buffer >> 32)` is a no-op (C# masks the shift count by &31, so >>32 == >>0), so the flushed bits are never cleared and high bits of straddling values are silently lost.
correctness.triggeringInput: bits=1, len=33, src = all 1s. Expected packed words dst[0]=0xFFFFFFFF, dst[1]=0x00000001. Actual: after i=31 the flush leaves buffer unchanged (0xFFFFFFFF) and bitCount=0, then i=32 ORs into the still-full buffer, yielding dst[1]=0xFFFFFFFF. Also bits=20,len=2,src={1,0xFFFFF}: bits 32..39 of the second value never enter the 32-bit buffer and are lost.
correctness.rootCause: `buffer` is `int` (32 bits) but the algorithm assumes it can retain up to 31 residual bits plus a new value before flushing; `src[i] << bitCount` discards bits beyond bit 31, and `buffer = (int)((uint)buffer >> 32)` evaluates to `buffer >> 0` (shift count masked to 0 per ECMA-335 / C# spec) instead of 0, so the word is never cleared after being emitted.
correctness.suggestedFix: Use a 64-bit accumulator: `ulong buffer; buffer |= (ulong)(uint)src[i] << bitCount; while (bitCount >= 32) { dst[outIdx++] = (int)(uint)buffer; buffer >>= 32; bitCount -= 32; }`. The final `buffer >>= 32` on a `ulong` shifts by a valid 0..63 count and correctly clears the emitted word.

correctness.summary: Bit unpacking corrupts values that straddle a 32-bit word boundary: residual bits sit in the low part of the 32-bit `buffer`, then `buffer |= src[i] << bitCount` shifts the new 32-bit word left by `bitCount` and loses its top `bitCount` bits, so values spanning two source words are reconstructed incorrectly.
correctness.triggeringInput: bits=20, len=2, srcLen=2, with a value packed across the word boundary (e.g. compressing {1, 0xFFFFF} then decompressing). The second decoded value comes back missing its top bits instead of 0xFFFFF.
correctness.rootCause: `buffer` is a 32-bit `int`; after extracting a value `bitCount` residual bits remain in `buffer`, and `buffer |= src[i] << bitCount` with `bitCount` up to `bits-1` shifts the freshly read 32-bit word past bit 31, discarding its high `bitCount` bits. A 32-bit accumulator cannot simultaneously hold leftover bits and a full incoming 32-bit word.
correctness.suggestedFix: Use a 64-bit accumulator: `ulong buffer; buffer |= (ulong)(uint)src[i] << bitCount; bitCount += 32; ... dst[outIdx++] = (int)(buffer & mask); buffer >>= bits; bitCount -= bits;` so no bits are dropped when residual and new word coexist.

correctness.summary: BitCount infinite-loops on any negative input because `x >>= 1` is an arithmetic (sign-propagating) shift, so negative values never reach 0.
correctness.triggeringInput: BitCount.Run(-1) (int overload) or BitCount.Run(-1L) (long overload): the loop condition `x != 0` is never satisfied because -1 >> 1 == -1, hanging forever.
correctness.rootCause: Population count is computed by repeatedly testing `x & 1` and doing `x >>= 1`; for signed types `>>` is arithmetic, so negative inputs sign-extend and the high bit is never cleared, producing an infinite loop. No contract restricts the input to non-negative.
correctness.suggestedFix: Use the unsigned/logical shift `>>>` (cast to uint/ulong first), e.g. iterate over `(uint)x` / `(ulong)x` with `x >>>= 1`, or use `System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount`.

correctness.summary: BitLength infinite-loops on any negative input because `x >>= 1` arithmetic-shifts a negative value, which never becomes 0.
correctness.triggeringInput: BitLength.Run(-1) or BitLength.Run(-1L): the while loop never terminates since -1 >> 1 == -1. This also makes NextBit.Run(0x80000000-pattern) and any caller passing a negative hang.
correctness.rootCause: Bit length is computed by counting how many `x >>= 1` operations are needed to reach 0; the signed arithmetic shift sign-extends negatives, so the loop never ends. No contract restricts input to non-negative.
correctness.suggestedFix: Use logical shift `>>>` (or cast to uint/ulong) so the sign bit is shifted out, or compute via `32 - LeadingZeroCount((uint)x)` / `64 - LeadingZeroCount((ulong)x)`.

perf.summary: Replace the O(bitwidth) loop popcount with a hardware/intrinsic-friendly SWAR or System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount.
perf.currentCost: Loop iterates once per set-or-cleared bit position up to 32/64 times, each iteration a shift, an AND, an add and a branch test (~32-64 dependent iterations, fully serial).
perf.proposedChange: Use System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount((uint)x) / ((ulong)x), or a branchless SWAR popcount (x = x - ((x>>1)&0x5555...); x = (x&0x3333...) + ((x>>2)&0x3333...); ... ; ((x * 0x0101...) >> 56)). Burst lowers PopCount to POPCNT/CNT.
perf.rationale: Constant ~5 instruction SWAR or single POPCNT vs up to 64 serial loop iterations; removes the data-dependent trip count and the per-iteration branch, dramatically shortening the dependency chain.
perf.risk: SWAR must use unsigned shifts ((uint)/(ulong)) to avoid sign-extension on negative inputs; current loop already terminates correctly for negatives only because >> on negative int eventually reaches -1 then... actually current code loops forever conceptually is avoided because x>>=1 on negative reaches -1 (never 0) -> the existing loop is already wrong for negative inputs, so SWAR/PopCount on the unsigned reinterpretation is the correct fix and matches intended semantics for non-negative inputs.

perf.summary: Replace the linear shift loop with a leading-zero-count based bit length.
perf.currentCost: Up to 31/63 serial iterations (increment + shift + compare) to find the position of the highest set bit.
perf.proposedChange: Return x == 0 ? 0 : 32 - BitOperations.LeadingZeroCount((uint)x) (and 64 - LZCNT for long). Burst maps LeadingZeroCount to LZCNT/CLZ.
perf.rationale: Single LZCNT instruction vs a serial loop of up to 63 dependent iterations; collapses an O(bitwidth) dependency chain to O(1).
perf.risk: Inputs are assumed non-negative (negative int would currently loop ~31 times and return 32); reinterpret as unsigned for LZCNT. Used by NextBit/PrevBit which only call with positive values, so behavior is preserved for valid inputs.

perf.summary: Hoist the loop-invariant mask computation out of the inner while loop.
perf.currentCost: int mask = (1 << bits) - 1; is recomputed on every inner-loop emit (a shift and a subtract per decoded element).
perf.proposedChange: Compute int mask = (1 << bits) - 1; once before the outer for loop and reuse it inside the inner while.
perf.rationale: bits is constant across the whole call, so the mask is a true loop invariant; hoisting removes one shift+sub from the hottest inner statement (per output element).
perf.risk: None; pure hoist of an invariant. Burst would likely hoist it anyway, but making it explicit is free and guarantees it.

perf.summary: buffer |= src[i] << bitCount with bitCount up to 31 then 'bitCount += 32' makes bitCount reach 63 while buffer is a 32-bit int, so high bits are lost; the accumulator should be 64-bit (ulong) to actually buffer 32 incoming bits on top of leftover bits.
perf.currentCost: When bitCount > 0 and a new 32-bit word is OR'd in at offset bitCount, bits shifted beyond bit 31 are discarded, and bitCount grows past 32 while only 32 bits of storage exist, corrupting subsequent extractions.
perf.proposedChange: Use ulong buffer; OR (ulong)(uint)src[i] << bitCount, extract with (int)(buffer & mask), buffer >>= bits, all in 64-bit so up to 31 leftover + 32 new bits fit.
perf.rationale: Correctness/robustness: a 64-bit accumulator is the standard for bit-unpacking where the carry-over plus a full word can exceed 32 bits; it also removes the implicit truncation hazard without extra cost on 64-bit targets.
perf.risk: This changes observable output for cases where leftover bitCount>0 — but those cases are currently incorrect; if the design guarantees bits divides 32 evenly and inputs never leave residue, the change is a no-op. State this guard explicitly: only equivalent when bitCount is always 0 at word boundaries; otherwise it is a bug fix, not a pure micro-opt.

perf.summary: buffer = (int)((uint)buffer >> 32) is a shift by 32 on a 32-bit value (undefined/no-op masked to shift-by-0 in IL -> yields buffer unchanged) and buffer & 0xFFFFFFFFu is the full word; the 32-bit accumulator cannot hold bits beyond a word so the same 64-bit accumulator fix applies.
perf.currentCost: Per flushed word: an AND with 0xFFFFFFFF (no-op mask) and a >>32 that does not clear the buffer as intended, leaving stale bits.
perf.proposedChange: Use ulong buffer; dst[outIdx++] = (int)(uint)buffer; buffer >>= 32; bitCount -= 32; so leftover bits are preserved across words.
perf.rationale: C# shift counts are taken mod 32 for int, so (uint)buffer >> 32 == buffer (a no-op), meaning the residual bits are never cleared — a 64-bit accumulator gives correct, branch-light packing and removes the pointless AND mask.
perf.risk: Changes output only for inputs where packing crosses word boundaries with residue (currently mishandled). If bits*len is always a multiple of 32 with no carry, it is equivalent; otherwise it is a correctness fix. Flag, do not silently apply.
